title: Ezekiel 42:1–14
context: The man guiding the prophet through the visionary temple brings him into the outer court and shows him two blocks of priestly rooms, north and south, built in three stories facing the separate place. The guide explains that these are holy rooms where the priests who are near to the LORD eat the most holy things and keep the meal offering, the sin offering, and the trespass offering, and where they change their garments before going out to the people (compare 44:19). The architectural details are hard to reconstruct, and translations differ at points. Readers in both traditions take the temple vision of chapters 40–48 in the ways named at 40:1–16: as a plan for a literal future temple, as a symbolic or ideal picture of God dwelling with his people, or as fulfilled in Christ and the church.

verses.text: Then he brought me out into the outer court, the way toward the north. Then he brought me into the room that was opposite the separate place, and which was opposite the building toward the north.
verses.arminianNotes: Then he brought me out into the outer court, the way toward the north. Arminian readers note that the prophet is led step by step, receiving the vision as it is shown rather than designing it himself.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers observe that the guide is the man with the measuring reed introduced in 40:3. The tour moves from the inner house outward, and the rooms described here lie toward the north.

verses.text: Facing the length of one hundred cubits was the north door, and the width was fifty cubits.
verses.arminianNotes: Facing the length of one hundred cubits was the north door, Arminian readers see the precise dimensions as a sign that worship in God’s house is ordered and deliberate, not left to chance.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that the building is one hundred cubits long and fifty wide. The exact layout is debated, but the measured order expresses the holiness of the place.

verses.text: Opposite the twenty cubits which belonged to the inner court, and opposite the pavement which belonged to the outer court, was gallery against gallery in the three stories.
verses.arminianNotes: was gallery against gallery in the three stories. Arminian readers see a building arranged in levels, its galleries facing one another between the inner and outer courts.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that the twenty cubits of the inner court and the pavement of the outer court frame the building. The details are difficult, and reconstructions differ.

verses.text: Before the rooms was a walk of ten cubits’ width inward, a way of one cubit; and their doors were toward the north.
verses.arminianNotes: Before the rooms was a walk of ten cubits’ width inward, Arminian readers see a passage giving access to the rooms, with doors facing north for those who serve there.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers observe that the way of one cubit is hard to picture, and translations vary at this point. The overall sense is of an orderly approach to the priestly rooms.

verses.text: Now the upper rooms were shorter; for the galleries took away from these more than from the lower and the middle in the building.
verses.arminianNotes: Now the upper rooms were shorter; Arminian readers see a practical design in which the galleries took space from the upper stories, so that each level was set back.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that the stepped structure recalls the side chambers of 41:6-7, though the arrangement here is distinct. The text describes rather than explains the design.

verses.text: For they were in three stories, and they didn’t have pillars as the pillars of the courts. Therefore the uppermost was set back more than the lowest and the middle from the ground.
verses.arminianNotes: For they were in three stories, and they didn’t have pillars as the pillars of the courts. Arminian readers see the lack of pillars as the reason the upper stories were set back.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers observe that the verse explains the stepped design of 42:5. Such detail underlines that the vision was given with care, whatever reading of the temple one takes.

verses.text: The wall that was outside by the side of the rooms, toward the outer court before the rooms, was fifty cubits long.
verses.arminianNotes: The wall that was outside by the side of the rooms, Arminian readers see a wall fifty cubits long separating the rooms from the outer court, preserving the holiness of the priestly space.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note the recurring concern for boundaries between holy and common space. The wall shields the priests’ rooms from the busy outer court where the people gather.

verses.text: For the length of the rooms that were in the outer court was fifty cubits. Behold, those facing the temple were one hundred cubits.
verses.arminianNotes: For the length of the rooms that were in the outer court was fifty cubits. Arminian readers see the contrast between rooms of fifty cubits and those facing the temple of one hundred.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers observe that the rooms nearer the temple are longer, perhaps reflecting their greater closeness to the holy place. The text gives the measurements without comment.

verses.text: From under these rooms was the entry on the east side, as one goes into them from the outer court.
verses.arminianNotes: From under these rooms was the entry on the east side, Arminian readers see an entrance provided from the outer court, so that the rooms could be reached in an orderly way.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that the eastern entry fits the vision’s orientation toward the east, the direction from which the glory of the God of Israel will return in 43:2.

verses.text: In the thickness of the wall of the court toward the east, before the separate place, and before the building, there were rooms.
verses.arminianNotes: In the thickness of the wall of the court toward the east, Arminian readers see a second set of rooms, matching those already described, placed before the separate place.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers observe that the parallel structures on both sides convey symmetry and order. Many translations read this second block as lying toward the south, corresponding to the northern rooms.

verses.text: The way before them was like the appearance of the rooms which were toward the north. Their length and width were the same. All their exits had the same arrangement and doors.
verses.arminianNotes: The way before them was like the appearance of the rooms which were toward the north. Arminian readers see the same design repeated, with matching length, width, exits, and doors.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that the repetition emphasizes completeness. The two blocks of rooms mirror one another, as 42:13 confirms by naming the north rooms and the south rooms.

verses.text: Like the doors of the rooms that were toward the south was a door at the head of the way, even the way directly before the wall toward the east, as one enters into them.
verses.arminianNotes: Like the doors of the rooms that were toward the south was a door at the head of the way, Arminian readers see an entrance placed where the way meets the eastern wall.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers observe that the detail is difficult to visualize. The point is that the southern rooms have the same orderly access as the northern ones.

verses.text: Then he said to me, “The north rooms and the south rooms, which are opposite the separate place, are the holy rooms, where the priests who are near to the LORD shall eat the most holy things. There they shall lay the most holy things, with the meal offering, the sin offering, and the trespass offering; for the place is holy.
verses.arminianNotes: Then he said to me, Arminian readers note that the guide now explains the purpose of the rooms: holy places where the priests who are near to the LORD eat the most holy things.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note the three offerings named: the meal offering, the sin offering, and the trespass offering. The place is holy because it serves the worship of the holy God.

verses.text: When the priests enter in, then they shall not go out of the holy place into the outer court until they lay their garments in which they minister there; for they are holy. Then they shall put on other garments, and shall approach that which is for the people.”
verses.arminianNotes: When the priests enter in, then they shall not go out of the holy place into the outer court until they lay their garments in which they minister there; Arminian readers see the care to keep holy and common distinct.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers compare 44:19, which gives a similar instruction about changing garments before going out to the people. Both traditions read the rule as teaching reverence in approaching God.
